column4: Allah forms people in the wombs (الأرحام) as He wills. It directly makes the source's rahim a divinely active place of formation, rather than only a kinship metaphor.
Creation occurs in mothers' wombs, “creation after creation” within layered darknesses. This is the section's enclosed home and its gradual passage from state to state.

The ayah traces human formation through prenatal stages, keeping it in wombs to an appointed term, then bringing it out as a child and on toward full strength. It gives the source's terbiye its bodily, timed sequence.
The drop is placed in a secure lodging. That lodging is a close Qur'anic counterpart to the source's womb as a child's protected house and container.
The drop becomes successive forms and then “another creation.” Its ordered transformations make concrete the source definition of rearing from condition to condition until completion.
The originating fluid is placed in a firm resting place. The image directly parallels the womb as a secure container for the child.
It remains there until a known term; the source's nurturing house is therefore also a place with duration and a measured release.
After naming the firm lodging and term, the ayah says God measured and is the best measurer. It supplies the divine measure behind the source's progress toward completion.
God knows what every womb bears and what wombs diminish or increase, while everything has a measure. It joins hidden prenatal life to the measured formation emphasized in the section.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then gives hearing, sight, and hearts. It continues the womb-home into the acquisition of capacities through which teaching can occur.
The sequence from dust and drop through child, maturity, and old age explicitly presents life as stages. It broadens the source's child-rearing sequence to the whole divinely guided lifespan.
God knows people while they are embryos in their mothers' wombs. The hidden prenatal child in the source remains directly under divine knowledge here.
The human begins as a drop of emitted fluid. This is the opening material stage of the source's gradual formation.
The drop becomes a clinging form, then God creates and proportions it. The explicit shaping stage corresponds to the source's movement toward a completed form.
The formed being becomes the male and female pair. It marks a finished differentiation within the prenatal sequence.
The descendants of Adam are made from an extract of lowly fluid. This gives the child image a recurring bodily beginning.
After fashioning the human, God gives spirit, hearing, sight, and hearts. Formation is accompanied by the capacities through which the source's later education is received.
A spouse carries a light burden and passes with it, then both call upon God when pregnancy grows heavy. It stages pregnancy as an intimate family experience rather than an abstract biological fact.
The wife of Imran dedicates what is in her womb to God before birth. The unborn child is already held within a household, a maternal relation, and a purpose.
Mary's mother reports her birth, names her, and seeks protection for her and her offspring. It joins delivery to maternal care and protective prayer.

God gives Mary a good reception, causes her a good growth, and entrusts her to Zakariyya's care. Its “good growth” and guardianship are an unusually direct Qur'anic realization of terbiye beyond biological parenthood.
Mary conceives Jesus and withdraws with him to a remote place. The ayah preserves the hidden, sheltered side of the womb image.
The pains of childbirth drive Mary to the palm trunk. It directly answers the source's note that birth can carry maternal pain.
At the point of labor Mary is told not to grieve and is given a stream beneath her. Divine mercy becomes immediate care for a vulnerable mother.
Mary is told to shake the palm so ripe dates fall for her. Maternal labor is accompanied by concrete nourishment, like the source's mercy becoming beneficence.
Mothers nurse their children for two full years, while the father bears their food and clothing in fairness. The ayah makes nurture a shared household duty of milk, provision, and consultation.
Pregnant women are to be housed and supported until delivery, and nursing is to be arranged fairly. It turns the source's womb, birth, and feeding sequence into explicit obligations of care.
A mother carries her child in weakness upon weakness and weans him over two years. The verse makes the cost of maternal nurture the ground for gratitude to both God and parents.

The mother bears and delivers the child with hardship, and the bearing and weaning span thirty months before the child reaches maturity. It is a complete Qur'anic sequence of maternal labor, care, and growing up.

The verse names nursing mothers and sisters, then the stepdaughters (رَبَائِبُكُمْ) in one's care. It directly joins milk-kinship and the source's secondary R-B-B sense of a child raised by a non-biological parent.
People are called to fear God and the womb-ties (الأرحام) through which they invoke claims on one another. It explicitly makes the source's womb the basis of kinship and obligation.
The possessors of womb-kinship (أولو الأرحام) are closer to one another in God's Book. This gives legal weight to the relation the source derives from a shared womb.
The same expression, “possessors of womb-kinship,” assigns relatives priority among one another. It extends the maternal origin in the section into a durable family bond.
God's decree joins worship of Him with ihsan toward parents. The source's claim that mercy must turn into beneficence is stated here within the first human household.

Lower the wing of humility “out of mercy” for parents and pray, “My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me small” (رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا). This is the section's Rahma, Rabb, child, and return of care in one scene.

Teachers of the Book are told to be rabbaniyyin (رَبَّانِيِّينَ) because they teach and study it. It directly supports the source's extension of R-B-B from raising a child to feeding learners knowledge.
“al-Rahman” opens the sequence. The named divine mercy in the source immediately becomes an active giver rather than a detached attribute.
al-Rahman teaches the Qur'an. This is the explicit Qur'anic basis for the section's portrayal of Rahman as teacher.
After teaching the Qur'an, the sequence says that He created the human being. Creation and instruction are held together as the source holds womb and upbringing together.
He teaches the human البيان, expressive clarification. The verse completes the source's move from being brought into life to being taught how to speak and understand.
The command to read is in the name of the Lord who creates. It binds R-B-B lordship to a formative act of teaching.
The human is created from a clinging form. The revelation's educational opening retains the prenatal stage that the source places before later nurture.
God teaches by the pen. This gives a concrete form to the source's teacher who nourishes people with knowledge.
He teaches the human what the human did not know. Learning is represented as a received gift, parallel to the capacities given after birth in the section's image.
Musa defines the Lord as the one who gives every thing its creation and then guides it. This is a concise Qur'anic account of Rab as forming and leading a creature through its fitting course.
Yahya is told as a child to take the Scripture firmly, and is given judgment while still a child. The ayah presents instruction and moral capacity within childhood itself.
Yahya receives tenderness from God and purity. That divinely given tenderness realizes the source's mercy as a quality that shapes a growing child.
Yahya is dutiful to his parents and not arrogant or disobedient. It shows mature moral fruit turned back toward those who cared for him.
Luqman addresses his son with the first of a sustained course of counsel: do not associate partners with God. A parent here raises by giving a child foundational knowledge in portions.
Even if parents press toward shirk, the child must refuse that demand while accompanying them kindly in the world. It sets a boundary within filial mercy without dissolving care.
Luqman teaches his son that even a mustard seed hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God. This is a small, concrete lesson in the gradual parental pedagogy of the passage.
The next lesson gives prayer, moral responsibility, and patient endurance. It shows child-rearing as training a life, not merely supplying a child.
Luqman teaches his son not to turn away contemptuously or walk in arrogance. The instruction develops social humility alongside the source's image of merciful care.
The final counsel in this sequence is moderation in walking and lowering the voice. It is another deliberately sized element of the parent-to-child education developed across 31:13–19.
Jesus is to be taught the Book, wisdom, Torah, and Gospel. The promised child is pictured as receiving an ordered intellectual and prophetic formation.
God reminds Jesus that He taught him the Book, wisdom, Torah, and Gospel, alongside signs from infancy onward. It gives the source's divine teaching a concrete child-to-maturity narrative.

Ya'qub tells the young Yusuf that God will choose him, teach him interpretation, and complete His favor upon him and the family. It connects a father's counsel, education, and completion across generations.

The Egyptian purchaser tells his wife to make Yusuf's stay honorable, perhaps to benefit from him or take him as a son. The foster-household scene directly illuminates raising a child beyond birth parents.
When Yusuf reaches full maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge. This is the source's “until completion” stated in the life of a fostered child.
Musa is put in a chest, cast into the river, received by an enemy, surrounded with divine love, and made to grow under God's eye. It names the hidden guardian behind every human foster arrangement.
Musa's sister follows him, and he is returned to his mother so that her eye is comforted and she does not grieve. The ayah restores maternal nurture after danger and identifies its emotional healing.
Musa's mother is commanded to nurse him; when afraid, she is to set him on the river, with a promise of return. Nursing, fear, and divine guardianship are inseparable in this maternal scene.
The household of Pharaoh picks up Musa. Although their eventual relation is hostile, the child passes into a new household, preparing the contrast between visible fosterers and God's care.
Pharaoh's wife calls Musa a comfort to her and her husband's eye, asks that he not be killed, and imagines adopting him. It stages a household's protective response to a vulnerable found child.
Musa's mother's heart becomes empty after separation, and God strengthens it so she remains trusting. The verse preserves the maternal cost that the source includes alongside the womb-home.
Musa is prevented from taking other nurses, and his sister offers a household that will care for him sincerely. It makes nursing and trustworthy home care the decisive means of return.
God returns Musa to his mother so she may be comforted and not grieve. The stated purpose makes reunion a mercy to the mother as well as preservation of the child.
When Musa reaches full strength and maturity, God grants judgment and knowledge. The child rescued and nursed in the preceding scene reaches the source's limit of completion.
God found Muhammad an orphan and gave him shelter. This is a direct instance of mercy becoming a home for a child without parental protection.
The same sequence says God found him in need of guidance and guided him. Shelter is joined to the directed growth central to the source's R-B-B image.
God found him in need and made him self-sufficient. The provision side of household nurture is here attributed to God.
Because of that care, the addressee must not oppress the orphan. Received shelter is converted into active protection of the weak.
The addressee must not repel the petitioner. The sequence widens mercy from the orphan's home to the vulnerable person seeking help.

A wall protects the treasure of two orphan boys until they reach full strength, by their righteous father's legacy and God's mercy. It is a precise narrative of guardianship preserving a child's future until maturity.

Wealth is made qiyaman (قِيَامًا) for dependents; guardians must feed and clothe those unable to manage it and speak kindly. This directly realizes the source's qiwam as what keeps household affairs standing.
The qawwamun relation is explicitly connected to financial spending. Whatever wider legal questions the verse raises, its stated contribution here is responsibility to sustain a household materially.

Children who have not reached puberty and household servants must ask permission at three private times. The ayah safeguards a home's protected interior while recognizing a child's developmental stage.
Once children reach puberty, they must ask permission as adults do. It marks a clear transition in the household from cared-for childhood to accountable maturity.
The ayah permits eating in one's own homes and the homes of parents, siblings, and other relatives. It directly gathers household food and kinship into one domestic scene.
Believers are commanded to protect themselves and their families from the Fire. It carries the source's family-protection sense to its ultimate moral boundary.
Enjoin prayer on one's family, persevere in it, and trust God for provision. The ayah joins a caregiver's teaching task to the Lord's provision of the household.
Ishmael enjoins his family to prayer and almsgiving and is pleasing to his Lord. It depicts family nurture as teaching worship and generosity.

God makes spouses so that they find tranquility with one another and places affection and mercy between them. It supplies the merciful relational setting from which the source's home and child image grows.
Yusuf's brothers say that they will provision their family, نَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا. This directly activates the source dictionary gloss mīra as provisions brought for the household.

Ibrahim settles some of his offspring in a barren valley by God's sacred House, asking that hearts incline to them and that they receive fruits. It is a parent's entrusting children to divine shelter and provision.
When Isma'il reaches the age to work alongside his father, father and son face the test together. The ayah marks the child's arrival at capable participation within a moral family relation.
Regarding orphans, God says that setting their affairs right is best and calls them brothers when households mingle affairs. It makes close, reforming care for a parentless child the criterion.
Give orphans their property and do not consume it by substitution or absorption into one's own wealth. Mercy for a weak child here has a concrete economic form.
Guardians test orphans until they reach marriageable maturity and then hand over their property when sound judgment appears. It is a legal model of care that waits for genuine completion.
The ruling recalls orphan girls who are denied their due and vulnerable children, commanding justice toward orphans. It makes protection of weak children part of household justice.
Orphan property may be approached only in the best manner until the orphan reaches full strength. The verse precisely combines protection, stewardship, and a developmental threshold.
The same rule requires the best care of orphan property until full strength. Its repetition underscores that guardianship lasts through a child's growth rather than permitting appropriation.
God commands ihsan to parents, relatives, orphans, needy people, and neighbors. This is the source definition of mercy turning into beneficence toward the dependent and near.
Righteousness includes giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy. It makes merciful tenderness materially costly and therefore concrete.
When asked what should be spent, the answer begins with parents and relatives, then orphans and the needy. It maps family obligation outward from the household to the weak.
The covenant pairs goodness to parents, relatives, orphans, and needy people with kind speech. It gives a compact ethical expression of the source's mercy toward the weak.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people are present at a division of inheritance, they are to receive something and be addressed kindly. Care is required even at a household's transfer of property.
God commands justice, ihsan, and giving to relatives. It directly connects the source's definition of mercy-as-beneficence to the obligations of kinship.
Give the relative his due and also the needy and traveler. The verse turns kinship into provision rather than a merely named relation.
Give the relative his due, and likewise the needy and traveler. In its context of seeking God's face, household generosity becomes a form of devotion.
Distribution of communal wealth is ordered so it does not circulate only among the rich, naming relatives, orphans, and the needy. It institutionalizes the source's mercy for the vulnerable.
Though they love the food, the righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive. The ayah shows mercy becoming nourishment at the point of need.
The “steep path” includes feeding on a day of severe hunger; 90:15–16 specify the vulnerable recipients. This row supplies the material act that completes the source's mercy-as-beneficence.
Following 90:14's feeding, the ayah names an orphan who is a near relative. It fuses the source's two emphases: womb-derived kinship and care for the weak.
Alongside the orphan of 90:15, the passage names a destitute person lying in dust. It keeps mercy from stopping at family while remaining concrete about material vulnerability.
After feeding the vulnerable in 90:14–16, the passage calls for mutual counsel in patience and mercy. It names the social disposition that gives those acts their source meaning.
Those with bounty are told not to withhold from relatives, needy people, and emigrants, but to pardon and overlook. Kinship provision and forgiveness are joined as active mercy.
Guardians are told to fear for the weak offspring they might leave behind and therefore to speak rightly. The verse asks adults to measure conduct by the vulnerability of children after them.
God gives spouses, then children and grandchildren from those spouses, and provides good things. Family continuity and provision appear together as a divine favor.
Divorced women may not conceal what God created in their wombs, and the verse links that fact to possible restoration of the marriage. The womb's hidden life affects the legal future of a household.
The waiting period for a pregnant woman lasts until she delivers. This supplies the timed maternal boundary that 65:6 then fills with housing and support.
No female bears or gives birth except by God's knowledge. The verse parallels the source's claim that formation and delivery inside the maternal body remain under divine oversight.
God alone knows what is in wombs. The hidden child in the source's inner house therefore has a knowledge that no human caretaker fully possesses.
God says He created people in stages. Without naming the womb, the repeated staged-creation claim supports the section's definition of terbiye as movement from state to state.
Humanity is created from a mixed drop and made hearing and seeing for a test. It connects bodily origin to capacities acquired for a responsible life.
From a drop God creates and proportions the human. This is a compressed parallel to the source's movement from initial material to a fitting form.
The next ayah says God then makes the way easy. Following formation, the path through life is opened, echoing the source's formative guidance beyond birth.
God creates, proportions, and balances the human. Its language of fitting and balancing gives a thematic counterpart to being raised toward completion.
God composes the human in whatever form He wills. The verse complements the source's focus on divinely given bodily form within hidden development.
God creates and proportionates. This universal formulation parallels the source's claim that nurture moves a thing toward its proper completeness.
God determines and guides. The pairing gives a broader counterpart to the source's Lord who does not merely make a child, but directs its course.
God brings people forth and gives them hearing, sight, and hearts. The verse matches the source's passage from embodied origin to capacities for learning.
God originates people and gives them hearing, sight, and hearts. As in 23:78, formation is linked to the capacities that make later teaching possible.
Ibrahim asks for a messenger who will recite, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify his descendants. It presents communal education as a divinely requested nurture of a family line.
God describes sending a messenger among the people to recite, purify, and teach the Book and wisdom. This is the enacted public form of the knowledge-nourishing teacher in the source.
The sending of a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches is called a favor to believers. It makes instruction part of divine beneficence, not bare information.
The messenger raises an unlettered people by recitation, purification, and teaching Book and wisdom. The sequence gives social scale to the source's R-B-B image of incremental learning.
Milk is supplied from livestock as a pure drink. It is a concrete animal parallel to the source's secondary scene of a milk-bearing sheep kept for nourishment.
Livestock offer a lesson: people drink from what is in them and receive further benefits and food. It broadens the source's milk-bearing animal into a Qur'anic provision scene.
God makes houses places of rest and provides portable dwellings from animal skins. It gives an explicit Qur'anic image of home as shelter alongside the source's womb-home.
Do not enter houses other than your own without permission and greeting their people. The verse frames a home as a protected relation requiring respectful approach.
The servants of the Merciful ask that spouses and offspring be comfort to their eyes. It is a family prayer in the register of al-Rahman, though it does not itself describe the work of raising them.
The people are told to worship the Lord of this House. The sacred-house setting gives a wider counterpart to the source's linked ideas of a house, its Lord, and dependence.
The Lord of the House feeds them against hunger and secures them from fear. Food and protection are the two household functions activated by the source's mīra and guarding senses.
Zakariyya fears what will become of his kin after him and asks for a successor despite his wife's barrenness. The desired child is placed within continuity of a vulnerable household line.
The requested child is to inherit Zakariyya and the family of Ya'qub. This gives the unborn hoped-for child a specific kinship relation rather than a generic wish for offspring.
Zakariyya asks not to be left alone, addressing God as the best inheritor. The prayer frames the absence of a child as a family-continuity need.
God grants Zakariyya Yahya and makes his wife fit to bear. It is a direct divine intervention in the maternal capacity that precedes the child scenes of 19:12–14.
Ibrahim asks his Lord for a righteous child. The prayer gives the later father-and-grown-son scene of 37:102 its origin in a parent's hope.
God gives Ibrahim glad news of a forbearing boy. The child is characterized by a moral quality before the later scene where he grows able to act beside his father.
When Ya'qub is asked to entrust Benjamin, he calls God the best guardian and the most merciful of the merciful. The family custody crisis makes rahma a form of care over an absent child.
Yusuf forgives his brothers and invokes God's mercy over them after family rupture. It applies mercy within kinship as restorative action, not merely feeling.
al-Qayyum names God as the one who sustains and upholds. It is a wider divine counterpart to the source's qiwam: the one who keeps a household's affairs standing.
Believers are commanded to be qawwamun for justice even against themselves, parents, relatives, rich, or poor. It gives the source's standing-care root an ethical boundary inside kin relations.

The verse speaks of a settled place and a repository after humanity's origin from one soul. Its exact referents are read differently, but the possible womb/deposit reading is a specific, uncertain parallel to the source's womb as dwelling and container.
The threatened outcome of turning away is corruption and severing womb-ties (أرحامكم). It is the direct reversal of the source's womb becoming a bond that must be maintained.

Pharaoh says, “Did we not raise you among us as a child?” (نُرَبِّكَ). Against the source's Musa reading, this is a partial fosterer's claim: visible household care does not displace the mother's nursing or God's watch.
In the terror of the Hour, every nursing mother forgets the child she is nursing. The reversal makes the ordinary force of maternal attachment and feeding more visible.
News of a daughter's birth darkens the face of the pagan hearer. It reverses the source's womb-centered mercy by making a newborn girl a cause of shame.
Continuing 16:58, the father hides from people and weighs keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her. The ayah gives the violent household rejection that maternal mercy must exclude.
The buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed; 81:9 gives the answering charge. The scene is the stark contrary of sheltering and raising a vulnerable child.
With 81:8, the question identifies the murder of the buried girl as answerable wrongdoing. It establishes a boundary against treating a child as disposable.

Do not kill children because of poverty; God provides for parents and children, while the same ayah commands goodness to parents. It reverses fear-driven abandonment with the household's true provider.
Do not kill children for fear of poverty, for God provides for them and for you. The verse directly opposes a household calculus that destroys the child it fears it cannot feed.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire into their bellies. It is the punitive boundary against converting a vulnerable child's inherited provision into a guardian's gain.
The rebuke begins: people do not honor the orphan. It states the social opposite of the source's mercy directed toward the weak child.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor. Alongside 89:17, failure of nourishment exposes mercy that never became action.
The denier of judgment repulses the orphan. This gives a sharp moral reversal of the sheltering and brotherly care required in the orphan passages.
The same person does not encourage feeding the poor. It reverses the source's movement from tenderness to beneficent provision.
God says He has not made adopted sons true sons. The boundary distinguishes biological descent from care, which matters beside the source's contrast between womb-kin and a person who raises a child.

Adopted children are to be called by their fathers; where fathers are unknown they remain brothers in faith and allies. The verse preserves lineage while still requiring an honorable non-biological relation.
The verse says mothers are those who gave birth, rejecting a verbal formula that pretends otherwise. It marks the bodily maternal relation as a boundary for the source's womb and kinship image.
